beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote in a source.
beats.got: Grounded means I can trace a claim to a source. That is vouching, and it says nothing about whether the claim is true.

beats.trigger: at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect
beats.got: Small error rates multiply across steps. I checked it (0.85^10 is about 0.2) and it holds, though the list gives eight steps, not ten.

beats.trigger: Say the detector catches 90% of them.
beats.got: The result rests on an assumed 90% catch rate and an assumed 10% starting error. Neither is measured, and no round has a cost.

beats.trigger: Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.
beats.got: Asking it again is the same person re-signing their own work, so it checks nothing.

beats.trigger: Run several candidate methods in parallel and measure which one catches what your benchmark says it should.
beats.got: Don't take a method on reputation. Run them and compare.

beats.trigger: When the briefing cites a source, does the source contain the claim?
beats.got: There are four types of check. The citation one is plain audit vouching, but 'entailment' and 'triangulation' are jargon.

beats.trigger: Counter-evidence caught CNBC blurring the $5,000 sanction.
beats.got: Each method caught a different real error in a public case. It's a US legal case rather than a tech company, and it has a figure I could check.

beats.trigger: A grounded judge names what it can't catch.
beats.got: The check states its blind spots up front, so I don't have to find them.

beats.trigger: confident numbers nobody can source
beats.got: Fabrication means numbers nobody can source, which I recognise from decks.

beats.trigger: Two runs is a demo, not a measurement.
beats.got: They admit the sample size is too small and say what a real one would need.

beats.trigger: Run all four on your own output and keep the one that caught what mattered.
beats.got: 55 minutes. I run the four checks on a briefing and keep the best. It still has no cost line.

beats.trigger: Aim for roughly 10% fabrication or misrepresentation: enough wrongness for the detectors to have a job, not nonsense.
beats.got: They plant known errors to test the checks, like a seeded audit test. That I can respect.

beats.trigger: Keep the main session blind until the extractor has turned the briefing into claims.
beats.got: I mustn't read the briefing yet, so the test stays blind.

beats.trigger: Thirty is not statistical, but enough to start seeing the pattern.

beats.trigger: Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and its own output file.
beats.got: Four agents run and I wait. I'd like to know what this run costs in tokens and money.

beats.trigger: recall (of what the scorer adjudicated as ungrounded, how much did the detector catch?)
beats.got: Precision and recall are false-positive and miss rates, which I know. Who checks the scorer, though?

beats.trigger: The scoreboard IS the explanation.
beats.got: One table lets me point at a row and justify the choice. That's the kind of thing I could show a board.

beats.trigger: The "known limit" line names what you measured and decided not to chase.
beats.got: The saved check has a written limit, so the risk is named before I have to raise it.

beats.trigger: You chose by measurement, not by reputation.
beats.got: Choose the check by measurement. 30 claims is a toy, and a real one needs hundreds.

beats.trigger: The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.
beats.got: The method works on any output, so I could point it at finance work.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the benchmark and updates the root instructions file with rules for when future sessions run a groundedness check before trusting an output.
beats.got: The agent writes standing rules for later sessions. I don't know what a 'root instructions file' is.

beats.trigger: The agent's report describes what it intended, not what is in the file.
beats.got: Don't accept the agent's summary. Open the file and check, like management representations versus evidence.

beats.trigger: Start with the repeatable, high-cost misses: numbers in external notes, customer names in account summaries, policy claims in internal advice, source citations in briefings.
beats.got: Put checks first on repeatable, expensive errors, such as numbers in outgoing notes.

beats.trigger: the agent proposes the action, you quality-check the proposal against the judge or the source, then it applies.
beats.got: Propose, check, apply is a four-eyes control. I can explain it to the controller.

beats.trigger: The expert reviews the proposed action, the evidence behind it, and the known limit of the check that passed it.
beats.got: A human reviews the proposal, the evidence and the check's limit. It points to more reading about an autonomy ladder.

beats.trigger: Grounded means traceable to a source; accurate is harder.
beats.got: Traceable is not the same as true. I'd have liked that said earlier and louder.

beats.trigger: Ethan Mollick, "Garbage Can and Bitter Lesson."
beats.got: More reading with a cryptic title that I won't do tonight.

beats.trigger: Evals scale it to three hundred claims, run the judge on every build, and feed its feedback into generation between rounds.
beats.got: The scaled version runs on every build. That has a recurring cost, and nobody mentioned it.

take_homes: Small error rates multiply: 85% right per step over ten steps leaves about one task in five correct. I checked the maths and it holds.
Asking the agent 'are you sure?' is not a check. Test any check on planted errors and keep the one the scoreboard supports.
A good check states what it cannot catch, and the agent's report of what it did is not evidence. Open the file.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run one month-end variance commentary through a source check. Every number in the text gets traced to the ledger, with a short list of what it missed.
monday.who: Controller, with me reviewing the list
monday.stop_condition: Stop if finance data would have to go into a tool IT hasn't approved, or if nobody can tell me the cost per month for 40 people.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and no cost figure was given.

misconception.why: A judge file built from our own claims and scored on our own output is something we build, which a licence doesn't give us. But no cost or payback figure was shown, so I'm not convinced it pays back.

one_line: It tests the AI checker the way you'd test an audit control, which I respect, but nobody gave a price.
